questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure App Service
questions.prompt: An App Service has access restrictions allowing only your office range, and HTTPS-only is on. A penetration tester reaches a deployment console from a coffee shop. Explain.
options: The rules take up to 24 hours to apply
The SCM/Kudu advanced tools site has its own rule set; restricting the main site does not restrict it
Access restrictions do not apply when HTTPS-only is enabled
The tester used the app's managed identity
questions.explanation: There are two sites to protect. The SCM site carries deployment and console access and is the more dangerous of the two. It has its own rules, with an option to inherit the main site's.
why_not: Timing is not the issue. The SCM site has its own rule set and was never restricted.
Access restrictions apply whether or not HTTPS-only is on. The gap is that the SCM site has separate rules.
A managed identity is how the app authenticates to other services. It does not let an outsider reach the console.
questions.scenario_clue: "deployment console" - that is the SCM/Kudu site, which has its own rules.
questions.misconception: That restricting an App Service app restricts every endpoint it has.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure Azure Web Application Firewall
questions.prompt: A WAF has been in place for three months with a current managed rule set, and the application was successfully exploited by SQL injection that the WAF logged. Most likely cause?
options: The rule set version is too old to include SQL injection rules
The policy is still in Detection mode, which logs and blocks nothing
The injection arrived over HTTP/2, which the WAF does not inspect
An exclusion was applied to the whole rule set
questions.explanation: Policies start in Detection mode. It fully evaluates and logs what it would have done and blocks nothing — Microsoft's own wording is that detection mode provides no protection. 'Configured but attacks still succeed' is usually this.
why_not: A current managed rule set includes SQL injection rules, and the WAF logged the attack, so a rule matched.
The WAF logged the injection, so it inspected the request. The problem is that Detection mode blocks nothing.
The WAF logged the attack, so the request was evaluated. An exclusion covering the whole rule set would not explain a logged match.
questions.scenario_clue: "logged" but the app "was successfully exploited" - the WAF saw it and did not block it.
questions.misconception: That a WAF which detects an attack also stops it.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure Azure Web Application Firewall
questions.prompt: Your WAF blocks legitimate requests carrying an authentication token in a header. Which tuning option, and what should you know about rule set upgrades?
options: Disable the rule; upgrades preserve disabled rules automatically
Add an exclusion for that request attribute; if you later change the rule set version in the portal, rule overrides and rule-level exclusions are reset, so carry them across by script or template
Add a custom rule allowing all requests with that header; custom rules run after managed rules
Switch to Detection mode until the vendor fixes the rule
questions.explanation: An exclusion removes one request attribute from evaluation, so the rule keeps protecting everything else. Tuning is tied to a rule set version: the portal resets rule-state overrides, action overrides and rule-level exclusions when you assign a new version, while PowerShell, the CLI, REST or a template can carry them across.
why_not: Disabling the rule stops it protecting all traffic, and a version change made in the portal resets rule-state overrides to the new version's defaults.
Custom rules run before managed rules, and an allow rule on that header would let any request carrying it skip inspection entirely.
Detection mode removes all blocking - for every rule and every request - to fix a false positive on one header.
questions.scenario_clue: "legitimate requests carrying an authentication token in a header" - one attribute needs excluding, not a whole rule.
questions.misconception: That disabling a rule is a safe way to fix one false positive.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Functions, including authentication and network access
questions.prompt: A Function uses the function authorization level, and the key is embedded in a partner's integration URL. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing, provided the URL is sent over HTTPS
The key is a bearer credential with no identity and no expiry, and it travels in URLs and logs - the SAS token problem in a new place; use platform authentication or API Management instead
Function keys expire after 90 days and will break the integration
Function keys cannot be used by external partners
questions.explanation: A function key identifies nobody: whoever holds it can call the function, it does not expire on its own, and in a URL it ends up in logs, tickets and browser history. Where the caller can hold a Microsoft Entra identity, put App Service authentication or API Management with validate-jwt in front.
why_not: HTTPS protects the key in transit, not once it sits in a partner's configuration, logs or history.
Function keys do not expire on their own - that is part of the problem.
External callers can use function keys. The issue is that the key carries no identity.
questions.scenario_clue: "key is embedded in a partner's integration URL" - a bearer secret in a URL.
questions.misconception: That HTTPS makes a shared key an acceptable credential.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Logic Apps
questions.prompt: A Logic App request trigger's callback URL was circulated in a ticket. What is the exposure, and what mitigations exist?
options: None — the URL is only an address and the workflow still authenticates the caller
The URL contains a shared access signature, so anyone holding it can run the workflow; mitigate with trigger IP restrictions, Microsoft Entra OAuth validation, or a gateway in front
The exposure is limited to read access on the run history
The workflow will reject the call unless the caller holds the Logic App Contributor role
questions.explanation: The callback URL is a credential, not an address. Mitigations in increasing strength are IP restrictions on the trigger, Entra OAuth validation on the request trigger, and putting API Management in front so the callback URL is never the public entry point.
why_not: The callback URL is a credential, not an address. It contains a shared access signature, so holding it is enough to run the workflow.
Anyone holding the URL can run the workflow, not just read its history.
The trigger does not check Azure roles. The signature in the URL is what authorizes the call.
questions.scenario_clue: "callback URL was circulated" - the URL contains a SAS, so it is the credential.
questions.misconception: That a workflow URL is just an address.

questions.sub_skill: Implement security policies for back-end API protection by using API Management
questions.prompt: You apply validate-jwt, rate limiting and IP filtering in API Management. What makes those policies real rather than advisory?
options: Enabling the Premium tier of API Management
Making API Management the only path to the backend - a private endpoint or network restriction, or a backend that accepts only the gateway's managed identity
Applying the policies at the product scope rather than the API scope
Requiring a subscription key in addition to the token
questions.explanation: If the backend is directly reachable, every gateway policy is optional from an attacker's point of view. The gateway must be the only path — the same argument as the AI gateway in 03-03.
why_not: A higher tier adds capacity and features, but a directly reachable backend still makes every gateway policy optional.
Policy scope decides which APIs a policy applies to. It does not stop callers going around the gateway.
A subscription key is another gateway control, equally optional if the backend can be reached directly.
questions.scenario_clue: "real rather than advisory" - the gateway must be the only path to the backend.
questions.misconception: That gateway policies protect a backend that can still be called directly.
